title: Decomposing Decision-Making, A Cognitive Dimension to Teacher Rehearsal gnitive-dimension-to-teacher-rehearsal/
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline argues that professional development's emphasis on rehearsal has focused too narrowly on the visible, behavioural 'moves' of teaching, at the expense of rehearsing the in-the-moment decision-making that underlies them. Drawing on Grossman et al.'s concept of decomposition, he proposes breaking common teaching situations -- like circulating to give live feedback during independent work -- into their constituent decisions, then modelling and narrating that decision-making explicitly with teachers. He argues this benefits novice teachers, experienced-but-not-expert teachers, and even expert teachers differently. He closes by citing his own 2024 study suggesting that 'recomposition' -- recombining decomposed elements into new sequences -- helps teachers transfer techniques to genuinely novel classroom situations, not just repeat rehearsed scenarios.
points: Cline's central critique of rehearsal-based PD: it risks confining teachers to practising only the visible behavioural 'moves' of teaching, while the harder, actual skill -- in-the-moment decision-making -- goes unrehearsed.
His method, decomposition, breaks a common teaching situation into its constituent decisions, which can then be modelled and narrated explicitly with teachers.

He argues decomposition serves three different teacher populations differently: exposing tacit expert decision-making to novices, surfacing unfamiliar alternatives to experienced-but-habitual teachers, and helping true experts articulate their own tacit knowledge.

Citing his own 2024 study, he argues 'recomposition' -- recombining decomposed elements into new sequences -- is what actually helps teachers transfer a technique to genuinely novel situations, not merely repeat a rehearsed scenario.
quotes: One key mechanism identified is rehearsal which means teachers get to practise performing a new technique or strategy before they get into the classroom and do it for real.
This approach may suffer two problems. Firstly, that we may be confined to rehearsing only the behavioural aspects of teaching, the visible 'moves' that a teacher makes.
One key ingredient is to increase awareness and understanding of the decision-making process itself through decomposition – breaking down a particular situation into a more granular set of decisions.
One of the reasons why simply going to observe another teacher often fails to improve someone's practice is because there isn't the accompanying decomposition of what happened in the classroom.

A recent study by Sims et al (2024) showed that decomposition followed by recomposition may increase the likelihood that teachers can transfer the application of teaching techniques to novel scenarios.
